title: Truth as a Compression Artifact in Language Model Training
claim: A common pairwise evaluation overstates a learned preference; scoring against the full error family shrinks the effect and exposes where it appears.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared y-axis, dotted chance baseline, error bars
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a y-axis running from 10 to 100 percent, with a dotted horizontal line at 50 marking frequency matching. The left panel, titled 'Denoising corpus, training problems', plots correct completion against model size from 3.5M to 86M parameters. A blue line for pair accuracy against random errors stays high, at about 72 to 89. A red line for mass against the full error family rises steeply from about 18 to 59 and crosses the chance line near 26M. A gray line for the coherent error stays just under 50. The right panel, titled 'Description-length ladder', plots mass on the correct completion against the number of stored offsets, L=1 to 64. Solid lines show the 86M model and dashed faded lines show the 3.5M model. The blue realized-string lines rise, while the red family lines stay flat or fall. All points have error bars. The eye goes first to the blue and red curves diverging against the dotted baseline.
caption: Left: the denoising grid under both measures (4 seeds). Comparing pairwise against the single realized error reports a large effect at every size; summing the generator's full support leaves an effect only at 86M, and the coherent condition sits just below the frequency-matching line throughout (a completion-length effect; the length-matched values approach chance). Right: the description-length ladder of Section [ref], where summing only the realized false string makes the share rise with the number of offsets the rule stores and summing the full family does not.
abstract: When a transformer is trained from scratch on corpora that solve the same mathematical problem both correctly and incorrectly, which solution does it prefer? The usual test is pairwise, and it is not neutral: when the error can take several forms, a model that merely reproduces training frequencies wins it without preferring anything. We instead score the correct completion against every string the error generator can produce, a share on which frequency matching scores exactly 0.500. At 86M parameters the correct completion holds 59.0% +/- 0.8% of the mass against random errors (59.4% on an independent corpus), where the single realized error gives 77.6% and pair accuracy 87.4%, a three- to fourfold overstatement of the excess above chance; below 86M the primary corpus shows no preference. The coherent false rules of the main corpora are not filtered at any size (43.5--48.8%; the shortfall below 0.5 is a completion-length effect). Two experiments built to identify a compression mechanism raise the pairwise measures while the summed share stays flat or falls: both are negative controls, and compression remains motivation, not a measured mechanism. With the scored false strings held fixed, a false rule whose selector the model can learn moves the correct share from 5 points above the null to 7 below (418M--3.08B), though the correct completion still outweighs the selected string. What these models leave unfiltered is consistent or learnable false structure (one single-rule corruption excepted), not falsehood as such.
